question: Shown that every state that adopted central planning produced shortages and repression, an advocate replies: 'But that was never REAL socialism — real socialism has not been tried.' Why does this reply fail as an argument?
answer: It disqualifies every real example in advance, so no outcome could ever count against it.
choices: It disqualifies every real example in advance, so no outcome could ever count against it.
It assumes whatever failed in the past is doomed to fail in every future too.
It answers the criticism by attacking the people who ran those states.
It rests on how noble the ideal feels rather than on what actually happened.
context: This is the no-true-Scotsman move (named by Antony Flew): a claim is rescued from every counterexample by redefining its terms so nothing can count as a failure. A claim that no possible evidence could refute isn't strong — it's empty. The record it waves away: roughly 65-100 million deaths (Black Book of Communism).

question: A speaker says her program 'just means treating everyone fairly.' Challenged on its race-based quotas, she answers 'So you're against fairness?' — then resumes defending the quotas. Why is this a bad argument?
answer: She defends a claim nobody disputes (fairness) to dodge the one under fire (the quotas).
choices: She defends a claim nobody disputes (fairness) to dodge the one under fire (the quotas).
She treats her own side's motives as automatically purer than her critic's.
She assumes one rule from her program must hold in every possible case.
She attacks the student's character instead of answering the objection.
context: A motte-and-bailey shelters a controversial claim (the 'bailey' — quotas) behind an easy one (the 'motte' — fairness), retreating to the safe claim when pressed and advancing the bold one when not. The tell: the disputed claim is never actually argued for.

question: An activist tells a quiet classmate: 'Silence is violence — by saying nothing, you are doing violence to the victims.' The classmate agrees silence can be wrong, but says this goes too far. What is her best objection?
answer: Choosing not to act is not the same as attacking — it treats inaction as a violent act.
choices: Choosing not to act is not the same as attacking — it treats inaction as a violent act.
Only hard evidence about the victims could settle it, not strong language.
One quiet student has no power to harm anyone, so the charge cannot apply.
Silence can never carry any moral weight, so the whole worry is empty.
context: The slogan equivocates on 'violence,' sliding from a physical attack to mere inaction. Beneath it is a real ethical line — DOING harm versus ALLOWING it (the act/omission distinction). Even those who think silence can be blameworthy resist calling it 'violence,' because that erases the difference between attacking someone and declining to act.

question: A panelist ends a debate: 'The science is settled — the real experts all agree, so there's nothing left to question.' Even if the experts are right, why is this a weak argument?
answer: Expert agreement isn't proof, and 'stop asking' reverses how science works.
choices: Expert agreement isn't proof, and 'stop asking' reverses how science works.
It assumes the experts are secretly hiding evidence pointing the other way.
It treats two possible views as the only options anyone could hold.
It answers the doubt by attacking the doubter's secret motives instead.
context: Expert consensus is real evidence — but it isn't proof, and treating it as grounds to halt inquiry inverts the scientific method, which advances precisely by re-opening 'settled' questions. The fallacy's name is appeal to authority; the deeper error is mistaking agreement for proof.

question: At a rally a speaker tells the crowd: 'If you are not marching with us, you are standing with the oppressor.' Why is that a weak claim?
answer: It allows only two boxes — ally or enemy — when many back the cause but doubt the march.
choices: It allows only two boxes — ally or enemy — when many back the cause but doubt the march.
It assumes the marchers must have purer motives than anyone watching.
It points to the size of the crowd as the reason the cause is right.
It treats one person's choice as enough to free the oppressed alone.
context: A false dilemma forces a pick between two options when others exist — here, between marching and siding with oppression, erasing everyone who shares the goal but questions the tactic. The repair is to ask whether those are really the only two options.

question: Sentenced to death in Athens, the old philosopher Socrates was offered a quiet escape from prison by wealthy friends who had bribed the guards. He refused. What reason did he give for staying?
answer: Breaking the city's laws to save himself would betray the justice he taught all his life.
choices: Breaking the city's laws to save himself would betray the justice he taught all his life.
He was too old and tired to start a new life in exile far from Athens.
He trusted the gods to snatch him from the poison cup at the last moment.
He wanted the shame of his death to fall on the men who had accused him.
context: Plato's Crito (~399 BC) records the argument: a citizen who accepts a city's protection owes obedience to its laws even when they wrong him — fleeing would make Socrates the lawbreaker his accusers had falsely called him. He drank the hemlock instead.

question: Diogenes the philosopher slept in a clay barrel and owned almost nothing. When Alexander the Great — the most powerful man alive — stood over him and offered him anything he wished, what did Diogenes ask for?
answer: For Alexander to step aside — he was blocking the sun.
choices: For Alexander to step aside — he was blocking the sun.
For a marble palace to replace his old clay barrel.
For command of Alexander's conquering army.
For gold enough to never work another day again.
context: The meeting (Greece, ~336 BC) is one of antiquity's famous scenes. Diogenes the Cynic taught that virtue lay in needing almost nothing — even an emperor's gifts were clutter. Alexander reportedly said, 'If I were not Alexander, I would wish to be Diogenes.'

question: A knight glances at the castle clock — it reads noon, and it truly IS noon. But the clock broke exactly twelve hours ago and has not moved since. Did the knight really KNOW the time?
answer: No — he was right only by luck; knowledge needs reasons that track the truth.
choices: No — he was right only by luck; knowledge needs reasons that track the truth.
Yes — his belief was true and he had no reason at all to doubt it.
Yes — a castle clock is a reliable instrument most of the time.
No — you can never truly know the time from any clock at all.
context: This is a stopped-clock version of Edmund Gettier's 1963 cases, which broke the old 'knowledge = justified true belief' formula: the belief is true and reasonable, yet true by accident. Most philosophers concluded knowledge also needs your reasons to connect to the fact in the right way.

question: A philosopher argues that a mother who pulls her own child from a fire before two strangers has done wrong — she should have saved the greater number. A knight disagrees. What is the knight's strongest reply?
answer: A mother's bond to her own child is a real moral duty, not a bias to be cancelled out.
choices: A mother's bond to her own child is a real moral duty, not a bias to be cancelled out.
Saving anyone at all is good enough; the number of lives never matters.
She acted on raw instinct, so right and wrong simply do not apply here.
Only the head-count matters, so the philosopher must be exactly right.
context: John Cottingham (Partiality and the Virtues, 1998) and Bernard Williams ('one thought too many') argue that agent-relative duties — to one's own child, kin, community — are morally grounded, not failures of impartiality. The greatest-number demand is the abstraction under pressure here, not the obvious truth.

question: Over many years every plank of a ship is slowly replaced. A shipwright saves the old planks and builds a second ship from them. Two ships now float. A sailor insists the rebuilt one is the original. Which view is the sailor using?
answer: Original-matter — a thing stays itself by keeping its original physical parts.
choices: Original-matter — a thing stays itself by keeping its original physical parts.
Continuity-of-form — it stays itself if its shape and use carry on unbroken.
Namer's-choice — whichever ship people keep calling 'the original' just is it.
No-fixed-self — there was never one true 'original' for either to be.
context: The Ship of Theseus (Plutarch, ~1st c. AD; sharpened by Hobbes, who added the second ship from the saved planks) pits same-matter against same-form intuitions about identity over time. Serious philosophers split, which is why the bank attributes the view to the sailor rather than declaring a winner.
